name: Fabricated Citations and Fact Checking
title: Fabricated Citations and Fact Checking
answer: Fabricated citations are references that look real but do not correspond to any published work, often produced when a language model generates a plausible but nonexistent paper title, author list, or DOI. Fact checking in this area covers verifying that every cited source exists, matches the claim it is attached to, and is represented accurately. The scope includes both accidental hallucination and deliberate citation padding, and it spans preprints, journal submissions, grant proposals, and policy documents. For the AI researcher, this is a core integrity problem because a single fake reference can undermine an otherwise sound argument.

sections.body: Fabricated citations are references that look real but do not correspond to any published work, often produced when a language model generates a plausible but nonexistent paper title, author list, or DOI. Fact checking in this area covers verifying that every cited source exists, matches the claim it is attached to, and is represented accurately. The scope includes both accidental hallucination and deliberate citation padding, and it spans preprints, journal submissions, grant proposals, and policy documents. For the AI researcher, this is a core integrity problem because a single fake reference can undermine an otherwise sound argument.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Citation checking runs on standard bibliographic infrastructure: DOI registries, library catalogues, publisher metadata, and full-text indexes. A verification pipeline typically queries these sources through APIs or local mirrors, then compares the returned record against the reference string. Some systems also use language models to parse unstructured citations into fields such as author, title, year, and venue before lookup. The work does not require specialised hardware; it is mostly a matter of reliable access to authoritative metadata and clean parsing code.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The basic method is to extract each reference from a document, normalise it, and query a trusted database for a matching record. If no record is found, the citation is flagged for human review; if a record is found, the checker verifies that the title, authors, year, and page numbers agree. More advanced approaches use retrieval-augmented generation to search a corpus and compare the cited claim against the actual abstract or full text. Human reviewers then adjudicate borderline cases, because automated matching can miss near-miss fabrications or legitimate but poorly indexed sources.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main risk is that fabricated citations enter the scholarly record and are then cited by others, creating a chain of false authority. Provenance matters because a reference is only as trustworthy as the record that confirms it, and a missing DOI or mismatched metadata is a warning sign rather than proof of fraud. Journals, funders, and institutions are beginning to require citation verification as part of submission and review, and some have added retraction notices for papers found to contain fake references. Rights concerns include the reputational harm to real authors whose names are attached to nonexistent papers, and the duty of researchers to correct the record when a fabrication is found.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Automated citation checking is likely to become a standard step in manuscript preparation, much like spell checking or plagiarism screening. Future tools may embed verification directly into writing assistants, so a reference is checked as soon as it is typed. Shared registries of known fake or retracted citations could help publishers and reviewers spot repeat offenders. There is also movement toward requiring machine-readable citation metadata, such as persistent identifiers for every reference, which would make verification faster and more reliable.
